issues.quote: supplies every method the interface lists, or when it derives from a class that does; if a listed method is missing, the code does not compile.
issues.text: Claim 1 carries the condition 'every member that has no default body'; the bullet drops it, and section 5 then says an interface can give a method a default body, so the two sentences disagree. Scratch build SDK 10.0.300: 'UsesDefault : IWithDefault { }' compiles although it supplies no 'Send' (the interface gives it a body); only bodiless members trigger CS0535 (interfaces.md l.86 '(unless the interface provides a default implementation)').
issues.fix: Replace the bullet with: "implements — a class implements an interface when it names the interface after its `:` and supplies every method the interface lists without a body, or when it derives from a class that does; if one of those is missing, the code does not compile."

issues.quote: Without either, the interface is one more file to keep in step with its class.
issues.text: The two sentences before it hedge with 'usually', as outline item 4 does; this one makes testing and a boundary the only possible reasons, so every other single-implementer interface is declared pure overhead. Stated as fact with no condition and no supporting document under versions.yaml. Quiz q5 does not depend on the exhaustive form.
issues.fix: Replace the sentence with: "Without such a reason, the interface is one more file to keep in step with its class."

issues.quote: Had the payment code asked for `NotifierBase`, the fake would have to derive from it and would run all three steps, printing included
issues.text: The samples never send anything: `Send` only formats, adds to `sent` and prints. The lesson does not say printing stands in for sending, and never says who reads `Sent` (line 9). So I wondered why a test could not just use a real `EmailNotifier` and check `Sent`; the only cost I can find is a printed line, which makes the case for the fake feel thin. The situation's 'without printing or sending anything' also came before I knew notifiers print.
issues.fix: Add one sentence after 'print it.' in the third paragraph of How it works saying that in the samples printing stands in for the real sending, and one clause after line 9's explanation saying what `Sent` is for (who reads it).

issues.quote: C# also lets an interface give a method a default body; `INotifier` does not, and even then an interface cannot hold a field like `sent`, so the skeleton still needs a class.
issues.text: This brings in a new idea, an interface method with a body, right after Core concepts said an interface 'says nothing about how it works' and the diagram said 'no body'. I then could not tell whether an interface can also hand out finished steps, which blurs summary line 1 ('an abstract class hands fields and finished steps'). The sentence does not explain it further.
issues.fix: Either drop the first clause and keep 'an interface cannot hold a field like `sent`, so the skeleton still needs a class', or add half a sentence saying why such a body still could not replace `NotifierBase`'s steps (they use `sent`).

issues.quote: An interface that only one class will ever implement is not wrong, but it needs a reason too. That reason is usually testing, where the fake is the second class
issues.text: Read literally this contradicts itself: if only one class will ever implement the interface, a fake cannot be a second class. I had to re-read to see that 'only one class' means one class in the real program. Summary line 5 and quiz q5 repeat the same wording.
issues.fix: Change 'only one class will ever implement' to 'only one class in the real program will implement', and use the same wording in summary line 5.

issues.quote: Line 5 says two things: `NotifierBase` is abstract, so it cannot be created with `new`, and it implements `INotifier`.
issues.text: This paragraph walks through lines 5, 7, 9, 11–16, 18, 21–25 and 27–31 and explains `private`, `IReadOnlyList<string>`, `abstract`, `protected` and `sealed` in one block. I had to read it twice, jumping back to the code each time.
issues.fix: Split the paragraph after '…so `sent` fits.': the first part covers the class line and its state, the second the shared steps, the open step and `EmailNotifier`.

issues.quote: When you meet an interface your own team wrote in front of one of its classes, it is usually there for that swap
issues.text: 'In front of' and 'behind' an interface (also 'email and SMS already sit behind it', Beginners' 'something behind it must be swapped', quiz q5) are never tied to the words the lesson defined. I paused to work out that 'behind' means 'implements it, and code calls it through the interface'.
issues.fix: At this first use, add a short clause: 'in front of one of its classes, meaning the class implements it and other code calls the class only through it'.

issues.quote: You notice this when such a class must be handed to code that asks for a `NotifierBase`: the compiler rejects a second class after the `:` with error `CS1721`.
issues.text: The previous sentence imagines `INotifier` turned into an abstract class; this sentence switches to the real `NotifierBase`. I had to re-read to see that the point is the same: code that asks for any class, the swapped `INotifier` or today's `NotifierBase`, shuts out a class that already has a base class.
issues.fix: Begin the sentence with 'The same happens today with `NotifierBase`, which is a class:' so the switch from the imagined swap to the real type is said out loud.

issues.quote: though the object it hands out is still the class's own list, unlike `OrderEncapsulated`, which hands out none
issues.text: I cannot tell why it matters that the object handed out is still the class's own list; the lesson does not say what other code could do with it. 'Hands out none' is also unclear: none of what, its lines? The encapsulation summary I know does not say.
issues.fix: Either add a few words saying what follows from it being the class's own list and what `OrderEncapsulated` does not hand out, or end the line after 'no method that adds to the `sent` list'.

issues.quote: each would be the only class behind its interface if one were added
issues.text: The stem says the class would be the only one behind its interface, but the correct explanation says the interface gets 'a second class to hold, the fake'. I could still pick (a), but the two sentences disagree and made me doubt my reading.
issues.fix: Change the stem to 'each would be the only class in the real program behind its interface if one were added' (both vi and en).

skipped_steps: How it works: the samples only print, yet the lesson never says printing stands in for sending or who reads `Sent`, so why a test needs a fake instead of a real `EmailNotifier` plus `Sent` is not reconstructed.
Đơn Hàng: 'C# also lets an interface give a method a default body' is introduced without saying what it changes for the contract/skeleton split.
Connections: 'the object it hands out is still the class's own list' is not followed by why that matters.
